utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, yesterday we left off discussing that activity, the military activity, of the SDA, or rather, its military wing, the Patriotic League. Now, I have to conclude my cross-examination today it seems, so to avoid me having to ask you to come back, would you allow me to ask the questions and you give yes or no answers. Now, do you agree that the adversary of the Patriotic League was the -- was the JNA and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So was it the Croats who were the enemies of the Patriotic League, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the Patriotic League when it was founded specified an adversary. Its purpose was stated as the defence of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From whom? You must have found that, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you that I have not found that. I do not know. I simply testify to you, in accord with your request that I give you straightforward answers, that at the time it was founded I don't believe an adversary was specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 65 ter 30570 next, please, on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, let me ask you, Dr. Donia, do you remember that 83 deputies Serbs, from a number of parties on the 9th of January proclaimed the founding of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 9th of January by the delegates in self-proclaimed Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that we continued to work together in organs, both in the Presidency, the government, and the joint Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where didn't we work then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say you didn't work. Your question was: Did we continue to work together? And it would be my interpretation that although the members of the SDS, for the most part, stayed in the organs of the government, Presidency, and Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not working together with others in those organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that they didn't work together, or rather, they only voted against the decisions that were to the detriment of the Serbian people, whereas other decisions were taken jointly, together; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did we take part in the joint session of the Assembly on the 24th and 25th of January?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs, the Serbian Assembly, all the deputies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the SDA deputies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And everybody else from the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my knowledge at least the vast majority did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at this document now on our screens. It's a conversation between Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic, a telephone conversation. And if you don't know, let me tell you that Jovica Stanisic was an intelligence officer and head of the intelligence service of Serbia. And here he mostly is keeping quiet and gathering knowledge and information from me. Now, this is page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to page 5 of the English which will be page 3 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And so that I don't have to read this out, I would like to turn to the first long paragraph spoken by Karadzic. Yes, 5 in English, lower down, the bigger paragraph, yes. Now, here you can see that I'm talking to Mr. Stanisic and I'm explaining to him how the conference is evolving. I say the conference started -- Wijnands, Ambassador Wijnands came to see me, and now I'm explaining to him and saying that Bosnia -- well, we then said that we do not want any division of Bosnia because it is both unpopular and unnecessary ultimately, because probably there will be no borders anywhere in Yugoslavia. May we move on to the next page. Page 6 in English, please. There will be rather a sort of administrative affiliation if there is no war. If there is war, if it goes on for 30 years, then nobody will win, nobody will recover from it, and we will all be impoverished and ruined. The next lengthy paragraph there says: "But if it is finished quickly ... I mean, this conversation was interesting and very useful and we believe that a lot can be done there." And then I said to a man who's very close to Tudjman that: "The Serbs and the Croats could resolve all their contentious issues in a month or two." I'm talking to Tudjman's man, not Boban's man. Now, were you aware of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we now have page 21 of the English displayed, please, and it is page 079 of the Serbian. It says "079" at the top. And in English it's page 21. Yes, that's right. And Karadzic says there: "On Friday, on Friday -- on Thursday we have the Deputies Club. We must prepare well. Maybe our delegation will go to the joint Assembly. Our Assembly delegation must be very large, numerous." And then Karadzic goes on to say: "... if the Muslims want, we can finish everything peacefully so that everybody is satisfied, and if they don't, there will be chaos." And then lower down, next page, please, he says that: "Everything depends on them." Page 22 in the English, please. Page 22, yes: "So now everything depends on them. And I don't think they would be dissatisfied. We think they would be very satisfied. It is very important what they'll finish or do in Turkey. I'm waiting to see that, to hear what will happen." "And then because I think there will be work here every day we must also continue the conference on Bosnia with lightning speed. I mean, very quickly. Although these talks are part of this conference, the general conference on Yugoslavia. "And we achieved important results which will suit the Muslims too." Now, do you not think that it was important for you to know about this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've actually taken note of the first part of the intercept that you've read, and to a lesser degree the second part as well. The first part speaks to your growing alliance with the Croats, particularly the Croats directly reporting to Tudjman, whom you'd previously seen as a reincarnation of the Ustasha and the source of racist dissatisfaction with the Serbs. And in particular, the agreement that Mr. Koljevic sought with President Tudjman in Zagreb on the 8th of January, just before the actual proclamation of the state, in which the two of them talked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- broadly about the division of Bosnia and the formation of new municipality lines, as well as the use of the state's -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, please don't interrupt the witness in the middle of his answer. Dr. Donia, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. To actually use the coercive powers of the state to enforce the human division in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, sir. But do you mean to say - and please give me a yes or no answer - that we shouldn't have negotiated with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was appropriate for you to negotiate behind the backs of the Muslims with the Croats about the division of a country in which they were a very significant political force. So I don't think it was -- the way in which you negotiated or Mr. Koljevic in this case negotiated was not appropriate. And, as a matter of fact, when you did this in May and negotiated an agreement in Grac without the participation of the Muslims, you were specifically reprimanded by the EC representatives for trying to cut a two-way deal when the rules of the conference and the negotiations were that any agreement had to have the endorsement of the three national communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, how could there have been the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina if all three parties had to give their agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- you've asked me about and I've responded to a situation in which you and the head of a neighbouring republic which had actually become a sovereign state were directly negotiating. I think that was not appropriate and isn't really a parallel situation to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was that the -- that two sides cannot out-vote a third side -- well, the HDZ and -- had the HDZ and the SDA made the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a federation of the Croats and Muslims later on without the Serbs, that's analogous; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 6th of May, did I talk to Tudjman or to Boban, which?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You met with Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Boban wasn't the head of state of Croatia, but the head of Herceg-Bosna; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe he was president of the HDZ at that point as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes -- well, yesterday -- let's look at this. Do you consider the departure of Kljujic, as Izetbegovic's man, was a rift in the HDZ when the HDZ remained with Boban, stood by Boban, and you said that Kljujic, the good Kljujic left and the bad Boban stayed. So we negotiated with the official majority HDZ party; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you negotiated with Tudjman's man, the person that Tudjman had put in charge of the HDZ in Bosnia after he had purged Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's not go into that. I told you that Boban won the elections, he wasn't appointed by Tudjman, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as usual. I'd now like to call up 65 ter 00023, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, with all due respect for you personally, I'm not asking you for your political views. I'm asking you for your scholarly, scientific views, to tell us what happened, not how you perceive it. Here we have the Assembly of the Serbian People on the 27th of March, and you know, I'm sure, that we managed to dovetail and co-ordinate the constitutional principles of the Lisbon Agreement on the 18th of March and a map as the starting point as the initial document; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, the previous document will be marked for identification as D301.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have to go back to one remark you made which is false, Dr. Karadzic, and that is that Boban won the elections. Stjepan Kljujic won the election on behalf of the HDZ in November of 1990, took his position in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and remained in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the Croat representative I think until about December 1993. Boban never won an election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the inter-party elections, that the HDZ was -- that the HDZ elected Boban. He was a respected leader, but that's not the subject we're discussing now. Do you agree that object on the 18th of March, that is to say that on that date the principles were established according to which for all three communities certain territories were recognised and that Bosnia would be composed of three constituent units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I have 65 ter 142, may I have 65 ter 142, please, first, the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that all remained to be dealt with was the map and the question of the army; otherwise, all the other principles were agreed upon. 1492 is the document I'd like to see before we look at this 27th of March document. And I apologise for stating the wrong number. 65 ter 1492 is the number. Is that right that the first stage of the conference was completed on the 18th of March by dovetailing and agreeing upon the constitutional principles?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without seeing the document, I can't agree with that. I think that probably the authoritative expression of your understanding of that agreement on the 18th of March is found in the opening pages, your words, in the 11th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, in which you repeatedly emphasised to the delegates that this was a negotiation still in progress, that the principles that had been agreed upon were quite limited, and that everything was, in effect, on hold. It was all expressed as something would happen, a state would be established, areas would be defined. And, in fact, when the issue came up of a -- the state becoming independent, you bragged that you had persuaded the other participants in the conference to adopt the language that it would be a state rather than it will be a state. So I don't think you're -- I don't believe that your representation of this agreement during the war was accurate, and I don't think your characterisation of it now is accurate. I think you were much closer to the mark when you described it at great length to the Bosnian Serb Assembly I think on the day after -- two days after the actual agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's not stick to my words or your words necessarily, but let's see what the document says and the words in the document. And this is what it says, what the document says. It was agreed that Bosnia would be and that I would accept the map and that people move out before an agreement was reached. I could not have done that nor would I have. So let's look at page 1 and then we can move on to page 2 to see what was envisaged for the constituent units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2 for the English. And we're going to tender this into evidence, but let's look at page 2 in English, "the constituent units." Let's see what their powers would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says -- well, it enumerates what they would be doing and then below it says: "The police, trade organisations, economic aspects, [In English] constituent units may establish and maintain relations and links with the other republics and with organisations in them, provided that these relations and links are consistent with the independence and the integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] And on the next page in English, please, it goes on to say, number 4: [In English] "All institutions (the civil services and judiciary, and so on) established by a constituent unit would reflect proportionally the national composition of the constituent units." [Interpretation] That was 3. And the next one says: [In English] "Members of the nations who would be in a minority in a particular constituent unit would receive protection similar to that in Article 2.3 of the draft Convention." [Interpretation] Do you say that we didn't celebrate this in the media, we and the Muslims, and the Muslims celebrated it even more than we did I believe; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender that into evidence and to look at 1D47 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has been already admitted as Prosecution Exhibit 782 through Ambassador Okun.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D47 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you said that I said it was a great day for Bosnia and that Bosnia had been saved. Is that what you said, or words to that effect, quoting me somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think your narcissism is showing. I don't believe I ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you could be a psychiatrist, more perhaps than a historian. Let's see what Ajanovic says here on behalf of the Party of Democratic Action: "The Muslims are satisfied with the statehood agreed upon." And now they believe that they will remain -- well, that they'll be a very small number in any minority. Now -- Ah, there is a translation. This is a statement by the vice-president of the Party of Democratic Action, he was a deputy in the federal parliament and his name is Irfan Ajanovic and he's celebrating. He says that the Muslims fared far better than the Serbs did. Did you know of this statement made by Ajanovic and their general attitude and standpoint on the 19th of March?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This in no way represents a general viewpoint of the SDA, and I have to say that I think that in the days immediately following the agreement and principle that you just cited, which wasn't signed by anybody and only represented an agreement amongst the party heads, that in the days after that just about every party had very widely differing views on the agreement itself. There was some disagreement within the SDS about the wisdom of the agreement. There was considerable difference of opinion within the SDA about the wisdom of the agreement. And, in fact, at a -- some sort of congress or party meeting within a few days afterwards, the party expressed its dissatisfaction with the agreement. There were some people who I think on every side, who felt it was a very positive agreement and a good step forward. And many people in all three national parties who felt it was not a good idea and it was strongly opposed by many people in the opposition. So there was, I think, a wide variety of responses to the agreement, a lot of concern about the numbers that you just cited, about essentially half the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina being left in areas in which they would be under the political domination of another group, and the very principle of division, which is something that the SDA itself came to oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, is this "Politika"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It looks like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a magazine as well, a "Politika" magazine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe there was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's "Politika," if I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic. Was Ajanovic a spokesman of the SDA at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Donia, whether you knew that the SDA had stated that, the officials of the SDA. In the evening they accepted, and the next day they stated this? Yes or no. There's no need for you to explain to me what happened with the agreement. We'll get to that. Did they celebrate and did I celebrate that agreement and did the Croats celebrate that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that any side unanimously celebrated the agreement, no. As I say, I think there were people who were very happy about it, others who were unhappy, and it didn't take very long for the SDA to come to fairly unanimous -- close to unanimous feeling that it was not a sound basis for further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this what they stated on the 19th? That is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what they stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this their official statement, and may I draw the attention of all participants to the second paragraph: [In English] "The Serbian Assembly would reject tonight's agreement with Jose Cutileiro. Ajanovic commented in his own way by saying that that would be the latest ridiculous act coming out of the Serbian kitchen. 'In that case it will become clear as to who is not for peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and who is cheating the European Community and the Chairman of the Conference on Bosnia,' said Ajanovic." [Interpretation] Ajanovic says that if the Serbian Assembly does not accept that, everyone will see who it is that is cheating the European Union, who is trying to deceive the European Union, and who is in favour of war and who is not. Is that not what he said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that this is "Politika" and they actually didn't carry the full text of his statement, they just carried a couple of exerts from it, I would say I'm not sure that that's the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have proof that "Oslobodjenje" carried something different and that he had not said this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the one with the documents, Dr. Karadzic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted for identification, and I'd like to call up 1D47 -- sorry, sorry, 47, this is 47. I'd like 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will be admitting that document. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't need further translations. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry, there is a translation. So 1D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this is one week later. That is what you had referred to. "Politika," again on the 26th of March. Nervousness in the SDA on the eve of the Brussels conference. SDA gives up on the agreement in Sarajevo. Can you see it? I'm going to read it out. Just a moment, please. [In English] "In response ..." [Interpretation] The second paragraph: "In response to the journalist's question why his party had recently accepted the agreement from Sarajevo, Ajanovic had responded that that was, conditionally speaking, a political game to ensure international recognition of a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this relation he said that his party did not want to reject the Sarajevo Agreement because it would possibly be blamed for the end of the talks under the supervision of the European Community, and the balance of power was three against one 'against the Muslims,' SDS, HDZ, and the EC were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining within its present borders, but provided that it is transformed territorially." Do you say that he did not say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply point out it's "Politika." As we sit here, a Serbian service called E-novine is re-running "Politika's" coverage of events on the eve of and early in the war with the sole purpose of showing how absurdly one-sided "Politika's" coverage was. And I think that alone should caution against taking anything that appears in "Politika" from that time with severe skepticism. And in the -- in this particular case you have again a story with a contentious headline, very limited quotations from the persons concerned, and obviously a political viewpoint being espoused in the article. So, on that basis, I can't agree with your proposition that that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to agree with my propositions. Is this what Ajanovic had stated, that he was buying time and that he had deceived the Serbs and the European Community? Is that not right? And you have that in "Politika" too. However, you did rely on "Politika" when you quoted Kadijevic and others. There are a lot of citations from "Politika" in the footnotes in your paper. I'm just asking you the following: Are you aware of the fact that Ajanovic said that they were buying time and that they deceived the European Community and the Serbs, yes or no, "Politika" has nothing to do with that. Give me a direct answer to my question. You're trying to evade it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question was what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is whether Ajanovic stated on the 19th they were happy, that they fared well, and that the Serbs would be blamed, and a week later he's the one who actually deceived them. Are you aware of that statement, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have the basis for concluding that he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Donia, you are totally ruining your own credibility. Is that right or is it not right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking him is that right or is that not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. No, it was not a question. Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you're doing pretty much doing what I expected you to do. And I think my responses are appropriate to someone who's using increasingly tendentious and biased sources to try to make the points he's making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the whole passage is not translated, we'll mark it for identification. So that will be marked for D303, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we remove the English version so that Mr. Donia can see what is written in the second part of this text on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, doesn't it say here that "so far over 1.000 shells have fallen on Bosanski Brod," just that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question: Does the headline state that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headline says that, yes. You read it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened on the 25th -- or actually, let me be more specific. Do you know that on the 25th of March in Bosanski Brod, armed formations from Croatia killed a father and a son at a gasoline station, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that on the 26th, the next day, this same column went on unhindered to Sijekovac and massacred entire Serb families there, everyone they could lay their hands on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain that it was the same unit or column as you call it. I certainly am aware of the events at Sijekovac and you're absolutely right, that was a brutal slaughter and one that deeply unsettled the political situation in Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us remove this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you quote "Politika" in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, you said I did. I don't recall quoting "Politika," but I'm not absolutely certain that I didn't quote it in the report on the formation of Republika Srpska. I don't have it in front of me, so if you'd like to give it to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'll be glad to give you an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll be losing time that way and the Trial Chamber can see that for themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender 49 -- or has it been MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 00023, that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I believe that this session, the 14th Session of the Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 27th of March is something that you are quite familiar with, yes or no; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that session, the Assembly established a council for national security?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- that's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that Assembly session the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was promulgated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 8 in English. We'll try to deal with this as briefly as possible. I would like to draw the attention of all the participants to my entire speech at that Assembly session, but we don't have more time now. So it's page 8 in English. "Before God," can we find that section, "before God and all men we stand ..." where there's a reference to God. That's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see a passage that "we are clean before God ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. It's the previous page. We should have the previous page on the screen. Page 7 in English, please. The last paragraph:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "We stand straight and pure before god! We wanted no division. We did not want the destruction of the things we had in common." [Interpretation] Now, there's no need for me to read it. Anyone can read this. What I'm doing is recapitulating our crisis, the crisis that culminated, we reached an agreement on the 15th. Mr. Donia, from the 15th of October, when we left the Assembly, did we remain open to a political solution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad you got to the point where you're pure before God and God is on your side. I think this is a very revealing passage about your position at that point. I think you continued to engage in talks up to that point, even as you were rapidly propelling the SDS and the various local municipal organs toward war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you are giving all these moralist and political and psychiatric comments more than scholarly, yesterday you said that Variant A and B were not responsive to this massive organisation of the Patriotic League. Would the right kind of response have been had we created a Patriotic League of our own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had an armed formation by that time, which was the SDS itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was that? You are saying something that is false, Mr. Donia. You could not have mentioned any in your papers except from a few from Serbia that came as guests, as it were. Do you know what their actual numbers were, those that had come from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear about four questions here and a couple of accusations --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're the one who's levelling accusations, Mr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, wait until you hear the answers from Dr. Donia. Let's proceed, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you kindly ask either one question or make one accusation, and I'll be glad to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Why in your paper could you not have mentioned -- or rather, you mentioned Croatian and Muslim paramilitary formations and not a single Serb paramilitary formation except for a few that came as guests from Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I used the word "guests from Serbia." I think I wrote a paragraph or perhaps two about the multiple military and paramilitary formations that were being created on Bosnian soil and gave a number which I took from Susan Woodward's estimate of -- along with the comment that there were paramilitaries being formed by every national group in Bosnia. And I think then I also talked about the fact that the JNA was at that time, had been for a long time, the dominant and decisive military force in the area. And I believe I also referenced the fact that it had become a -- kind of an open organisation to any and all volunteers that were either mobilised by Serb municipal authorities or otherwise recruited in conjunction with your efforts on behalf of Milosevic to add strength to the JNA in Croatia. That's my recollection of what I wrote. Again, if we're going to talk about what I wrote, I'd really like to have it in front of me so that I don't have to speculate on stuff I wrote five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you. We're going to find that now. You said what it was that the HDZ had established, what the SDA had established, and that includes the HOS and the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. For the Serbs you said in Bosnia-Herzegovina that some groups from Serbia had come to them, but you could not mention the name of any Serb paramilitary formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right? Can you mention one today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Hello, Your Honour. I've -- given that Dr. Donia has just asked to have his report in front of me, I just wanted to note that I have all three of them on offer and that may assist all of us in being able to identify which passages or reports, indeed, we might be referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he has answered -- the witness has answered to this question already. Let's move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 40, military preparations, Siege of Sarajevo, and then you say that the SDA sponsored two paramilitary groups, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. Do you know that up until the beginning of the war the Patriotic League had about 20.000 [as interpreted] people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I think yesterday you were complaining that I didn't note these paramilitary formations by the SDA, and now you see that I have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to reiterate my request to have the paper in front of me if I'm being asked about its contents. It's really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 120.000 is what the transcript should say. So it is the fifth chapter and the heading is "Military Preparations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 40 of your Sarajevo report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I note the -- I note the -- the paragraph that we're in here does indeed speak about the Green Berets and Patriotic League. I mention the number of Muslim representatives selected by the SDA and in the formation of the Council for National Defence, which we spoke about yesterday. Mentioned HOS, which was, of course, a very important and very, I would say, out-of-control and disruptive organisation that operated quite freely in Bosnia. The ZNG which operated less so, but nevertheless was a major force. And then mention several Serb paramilitary organisations without giving them a name, and indicated with a reference to Susan Woodward, who's about the most pro-Serb scholar one can find these days, the reference about those paramilitaries. The question of numbers at any point along the time line here is, for me, really unknowable. There are some estimates, as you noted, that there were about 100.000 or 200.000 or some huge numbers of people in these paramilitaries. I think it's really difficult to know. They were probably much more conspicuous by some of their activities than by the sheer numbers that one could attribute to them. In part because the vector sort of changed after the war and a lot of people who were commenting on the numbers had a great incentive to inflate the numbers of people who were in these paramilitaries because they were trying to claim credit amongst their co-nationals for the foresight of organising defence and advance. So I'm certainly open to looking at numbers, but to me the question of numbers is real elusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have for a moment 65 ter number 31670. Just one sentence. Let us have a look at just one sentence. This is an intercepted conversation of mine with Radic, I think. English page number 3. So we'll be going back to this Assembly session soon, but let us just see this 31670, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it says we do not have -- is this page 3? [In English] "It's a matter for the army. We -- we, our party doesn't have an army, and if any of our members want to defend the country, we are asking them to join the army." [Interpretation] This is the 11th of November, 1991. I'm talking to Radislav Vukic, and later on Predrag Radic and Brdjanin. Radic was the mayor of Banja Luka. So you see on the 18th of November, when -- while conducting this private conversation I'm telling my associates who wants to defend the country should join the army. Apart from the SDS - and you are saying in an unjustified way that they had paramilitary formations - is it not true that you cannot mention a single Serb paramilitary organisation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this intercept is very consistent with what I've stated to be the case, namely, that the SDS was in the business of mobilising, recruiting, and putting volunteers into the JNA in response to your urging and -- which was in turn a response to Milosevic's urging to bolster the JNA's war in Croatia. And also at this time you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that illegal, Mr. Donia? You are wasting my time --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to just point out that also at this time you were making sure that the people in the Bosnian Krajina were not themselves about to go off and march on their own to join the war in Croatia. And that was very critical, I think, to maintaining the position that you were trying to bring the JNA onto your side to effectively become the army of the Serb people; and on the other hand trying to avoid formation of a separate Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this. When I refer to Tudjman, that is 23: [In English] "It is out of the question to base our policies, base them on criminals, let Tudjman do that." [Interpretation] Dr. Donia, just one question, do you believe, yes or no, do you believe that my support to the regular federal army was unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the last passage you read out is not correctly reflected because you abruptly changed from Serbo-Croat to English. So what you said is: "It's out of the question to base our policies, base them on criminals ..." that's the passage. And then we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this makes Exhibit D3 -- MFI D304.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It exists in Serbian and English: [In English] "It's out of the question to base our policies, base them on criminals, let Tudjman do that." [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may we go back to that Assembly meeting, 00023 is the 65 ter number. Now I would like to ask you to focus on Radovan Karadzic's speech because there we have a recapitulation of everything, everything we experienced from the elections to the point in time when the Muslim side, or rather, the SDA reneged on what we had agreed. Do you see that in this speech I still hold out hope that there won't be a war and that an agreement will be reached. I'm sure you're familiar with that speech of mine. And I'd like us to look at page 8 of the English, please. Or rather, may we turn to page 20 in English and then 21, and I hope -- no, this is fine, actually. It says: [In English] "We cannot comprehend how they dared to reconcile with the Ustashas, the Muslim people, who rose against the Ustashas during this war ..." [Interpretation] The Second World War that is, [In English] "with the expectations [sic ] expectations, however, which were not few in number. There were many exceptions. But the dictatorship prevailing in the mass media is such that their voices cannot be heard. One cannot hear Zulfikarpasic who does not even dare to live here. The voices of Galijasevic's and Hasan Delic's, Yugoslav Muslim organisation, are quiet. Prominent individuals cannot be heard because the furry of those who have been and who are bent on attaining their goals is horrifying and their revenge would surely be vented on those whom they considered traitors." [Interpretation] Did you notice this part of the speech, when it says that no opposition from the SDA can be heard, that people, prominent people such as Zulfikarpasic fled to Switzerland because he didn't dare continue living there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with your speech as a whole, and again I say it's been a while since I looked at it. But, I think this is what you do best, combine these very proclamations of specific intent with some real sabre rattling and efforts to discredit your political opponents. Zulfikarpasic lived in Zurich, I think that's why he returned there. I don't think he moved permanently to Sarajevo until sometime in the late 1980s. I think your description here of what was happening amongst other Muslims is just an invention. So I just see this as a very --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're guessing now. You're guessing. What I'm asking you is: Do you know that I said that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... proclaim what your understanding of the situation was and effort to motivate people to support your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we look at page 20 and then page 21?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Doctor, you would be able to read the transcript. Could you take a quick look whether some parts are missing or not. Because of the overlapping of the accused, some parts of your answer were not reflected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you're saying, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were interrupted when you say, "I just see this as a very ...," and you continued from, "What your understanding ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was saying it was a very tendentious representation of the position of those Muslims who were in opposition parties, that -- at least words to the effect that these dissents were perfectly free to exercise any opinions they wanted to, and this is absolutely -- it's a fantasy, his description of what the situation was with these people who were not in the SDA but were prominent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue. In the meantime, the previous intercept 31670 was already either admitted or marked for identification as P4. So there's no need to admit it separately. Do you like to tender this minute, 23? 14th Session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly. It's a very important Assembly session. May we now look at page 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go on then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] "A war in Bosnia." [Interpretation] Penultimate paragraph: "A war in Bosnia and Herzegovina will not solve anything. If it breaks out, you will get the plans. But I urge you to immediately organise the people within the Territorial Defence units headed by reserve officers, form squads, platoons and Crisis Staffs, and engage retired officers. This must be done throughout our areas. "The presidents of the municipalities and Executive Boards will hold the highest ranks in the Crisis Staffs in addition to reserve officers. We must study the situation regarding the saving of lives, property, and territory. We have no other plans." So that is a response to somebody who is asking what happens when a war breaks out, will we get some other plans. And I say that there will be no other plans except to preserve and safe-guard lives, property, and territory. So I would like to draw your attention to the whole speech there, but we can move on to page 21 now. The portion about the Crisis Staff is there and there's another sentence which I would like to focus upon. "We are certain that nothing can be achieved by war, that they can't do anything to us. There are as many of us as there are of them, adults. "And according to our information, the Croats do not really aspire to Serbian territories."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So here we're hoping that there won't be a war, but, Mr. Donia, we propose the introduction of Crisis Staffs and strengthening the Territorial Defence should we be attacked. Did you put that in our [as interpreted] report, that it was only on the 27th of March that we recommended that Crisis Staffs be introduced and that the Territorial Defence should be strengthened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you had -- first of all, this is almost word for word from the A/B instructions. It's obviously the pulling of the trigger to actually go ahead and implement A/B, including the references to the reserve officers, the assignment of military responsibilities to SDS civilians. I don't think it could be any clearer. A little bit of a sanitised version because it doesn't cite those specific provisions in the A/B document which were offensive which were intended to seize the resources of the municipalities and take-over institutions. But I think that's -- that's pretty much what it is. It seems to me also you have here the indication that you, the SDS, that is, and the HDZ are moving closer to an alliance. You've basically agreed in principle here as much as a month and a half ago on the principle of division, of re-ordering municipal boundaries, and separating people one way or another through the use of governments, coercive forces or force, and that you're now to the point where you and the Croats have reached an agreement that there's not really a conflict between the territorial claims that respectively you're initiating on Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that are you taking into account that in 103 municipalities we have 13 staffs and 13 units and 9 -- 103 -- and 9 staffs at the Patriotic League with 120.000 armed Muslims? Are you taking that into account or have you forgotten all that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you don't address it here and I didn't address it in my comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do I have to tell my deputies something we know about - and we know about this -- and this is the question: Do you remember that the difficulties of living with the Muslims I linked and tied to the appearance of the fundamentalism phenomenon. Do you know that I linked it up to the appearance of fundamentalism?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you did that starting shortly after the elections, but it wasn't a major theme, as I see it, until about this time when you were really starting to get much closer to the HDZ and Tudjman because you really couldn't use that canard that the HDZ and the SDA were just reincarnations of the Ustasha. That wouldn't work anymore when you were trying to get together with the HDZ and the Croats. So the slogan of Islamic fundamentalism sort of came to the fore as something that could be an accusation that could be directed more specifically at the Muslims, as you and the Croats came into an alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the moment I'm not asking your opinions. If the Trial Chamber calls you back, then perhaps we'll go into that, but I'm just asking you for yes or no answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you a few questions, Mr. Donia, because you're not giving up on your sweeping statements that I see are completely unfounded. Let me ask you this: Is it correct that the SDA planned its projects based on Islamic and especially fundamentalist regimes in the world? Just yes or no. Any answer will suffice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender the previous document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can use the previous number. So it will be Exhibit D304. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, were you asked to be biassed and politically determined in writing your report? I'll accept any answer, either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you asked to be objective and scholarly, with a scientific approach?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to prepare an objective report on the topics within the time-frame that the Prosecution specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have here a letter from the distinguished Ms. Edgerton to you, which asks for you to do what you're asked to do -- well, it's your choice. It wasn't the OTP asking you to deal with certain matters in one way or another, but it was your recommendation. Yes or no? Is it your choice? Was it your choice to decide how you were going to go about what you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was subject of discussion between us, and I made certain suggestions. She made certain suggestions. And in the end we agreed on what it was that she would ask me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you asked to throw light on the events and to characterise them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you then think that this Trial Chamber is necessary at all because you seem to have created the indictment and done the sentencing and the judgement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's simply a comment. You know very well that this is an expert witness. If you don't agree with what he wrote in his report, that's all very well and you can challenge it. But making comments like this is simply wasting part of the little time you have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, were you able to throw light on every phenomenon, incident, and so on? Were you successful in that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for the most part, do you think that you elucidated matters and characterised them properly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, we were talking about methodology. I attempted to identify what I believe were the major trends and developments of the time, elucidate them, show what -- at least some of their causes were, and track the development of them. That obviously is a process that relies heavily on individual events and episodes, but doesn't pretend to cover all of them comprehensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at the beginning of your report you said that you wouldn't deal with constitutional and legal matters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report are you talking about? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The work -- one of the works -- well, at the very beginning I think you said when we came to the origins of Republika Srpska, you said you wouldn't deal with constitutional and legal matters because you weren't a constitutional and legal expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Words to the effect of -- to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in all this, did you ever hear the other side, what the other side had to say? The audiatur et altera pars from Roman law, so did you hear what the altera, other side, had to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What other side are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb side that stands accused. Did you hear that side and take into account what that side said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a couple of months going through the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions and many of the intercepts. I think I spent a lot more time listening to what the Bosnian Serb position was than I did the positions of any of the other sides, either the SDA or the HDZ or the sort of civic opposition, democratic opposition. Certainly made every effort to obtain an understanding of what the Bosnian Serb position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you said that the Serb actions were coincidental with the Muslims -- coincided with the Muslims. Now, did you establish and differentiate which of those actions of ours were simultaneous and coincided with the other sides and what actions the SDA took and when?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've said this before in answer to -- basically the same question is I noted that you had said this on two different occasions, that you waited for Alija to take a step and then you took a step. So there was, a way you described it, kind of a pre-established course of action that would be triggered by some action on the part of the other side. And I think some of these are almost self-evidently apparent. The manner in which you declared the preparations for a Bosnian Serb state on the 21st of December and indicated it would be contingent upon the decision on independence or recognition of independence -- I mean, now I think was pretty clearly a statement -- a preparation waiting for the triggering event and then going ahead with the actual event. I honestly didn't bother to or I didn't go through and identify what the triggering event was in each case. As I say, I think in some cases it was pretty evident and in other cases it was not. You spoke about eight or ten incidents. I didn't really see that many incidents in which that was the case, but you had said it so I chose to believe you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to take a break. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I could just speak to you on again a small administrative matter essentially relating to an exhibit we dealt with yesterday or a proposed exhibit, 1D01362. And that was what we -- that document was an extract from a publication and Dr. Donia had questioned the authenticity of this. So we undertook to try and locate it in house. I addressed, Your Honours, and said we hadn't found the transcript, the original transcript, from which this publication was excerpted, and I just wanted to confirm that, but one of my industrious colleagues has continued looking and found minutes, not the transcript, but minutes of the meeting in question which -- I was advised of this while we were sitting here in court today, which we disclosed immediately to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson, in the event it would be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your works -- or let me say that there are differences between your books and your other works on this same subject, yes or no? Are there things that are included in the books but that you haven't included in this report or let me say expert report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that you said more there than you did in the report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depended a little on the topic I would say. The book is or the books are probably more voluminous, if you will, much longer, move closer toward being more comprehensive and at the same time cover much longer time-periods than the reports I've submitted for this case. So in some sense -- in some areas they are fairly superficial in terms of their treatment of the events that we've been talking about the last, I think it's three months now, and at the same time in some areas may be more, let's say, put into a lengthier chronological context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your book "Sarajevo, the biography of a city," on page 340 and 341, did you write the following: "For months the operatives of the BH army hid the gunpowder in oxygen containers which the UN transported and which were officially intended for the city hospitals ..." et cetera, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they don't have the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just ask for the volume of the book because I'm looking at page 340 and 341 and I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's an English and a Bosnian translation of the book, so I suspect you're looking at the English, whereas Dr. Karadzic was looking at the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Doctor is able to answer the question without referring -- looking at the actual text of the book, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did write those words, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, do you testify and say that you saw the secret throwing in of weapons from Iran and other Muslim countries and that the scope of those operations is difficult to evaluate, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't say that in your study. You didn't include that in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I did not include the story of the oxygen containers in the report. I don't recall whether I may have referenced the import of weapons from Iran. I just don't recall. I'd be glad to look at it if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 345 and 346 of the Serbian version you describe an incident which occurred on the 27th of May and you stated that: "The Army of Republika Srpska shot three mortar shells in Vases Miskin Street in the bread line ..." et cetera. Why don't you describe that in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have tried to put these things in a -- in a narrative flow and in -- or to moving from writing this in a book format to preparing the expert report, I tried to be pretty circumspect in terms of what I included as being directly associated with the causation and development of the events I was describing. I don't specifically remember as I was writing weighing putting that in or not. It was my intention in the report to capture the broad sweep of events, and I guess that just didn't quite come to the level of meeting the criteria that I'd set out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, did you say that the Army of Republika Srpska shot three mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what Mr. Donia said, claimed, but it's well an incident and we claim the exact opposite. And as it's not believable the way he put it, that's why it's not in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 351, page 3-5-1, did you write the following: "Nonetheless, during the year of poverty in which the citizens were afraid daily, the -- they realised -- the citizens of Sarajevo realised that they were at the front line of bestiality ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or words to that effect, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer that question, you may wish to answer to the comment Mr. Karadzic made to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would fully expect you to have a different understanding of that event than I did. I know that that is a heavily contested event in terms of the -- who actually fired the shots. I was convinced sufficiently by the UN reports and other things that I was seeing to include it in the book, but I didn't want it to -- and I didn't want to enter it here in one of my reports and make it the subject of dispute when I knew it would be disputed by you at other -- with other witnesses and on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And coming back to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is -- I frankly don't remember this sentence. If you have a page or something that I could look at, I have a feeling there may be a translation issue in that "the citizens of Sarajevo realised that they were at the front line of bestiality ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 351 --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you have -- I don't have a copy of the book in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian the page is 351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to put it on the ELMO or do you have it in e-court? Otherwise, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 352, did you write the following: "In the months after the beginning of the siege, many Serbs left the city as the shelling and sniper activity increased, and some of them were killed at the hands of the Bosniak or Croatian paramilitaries operating in the city. In Pofalic street or in the battle of Pofalic in May 1992, the paramilitary units under the command of the BH Army killed, incarcerated, and beat a certain number of Serbs." As a historian, should you have established that certain number of Serbs, what number it was exactly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there have been a lot of efforts to establish the number of Serbs who were killed in that assault and more generally in the city. And I think there actually are some demographers who may appear in this proceeding who have a better idea than I do of even what the approximate numbers are. But unfortunately, there's been a kind of political gridlock in the investigation process as -- and I have to say I don't think it was entirely one side or the other. Either the Serb Republika Srpska side or the Federation side that have stalled this investigation into Serb deaths in Sarajevo and never really been able to reach a satisfactory number. I wish I could reach a number that's even an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it clear that on the 15th of May, 1992, the paramilitaries of the SDA attacked the Serb settlement of Pofalic, the civilians there, and killed a certain number without mentioning the exact number? Is there any doubt about who the attackers were and who the victims were, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there's some doubt. Pofalici was a mixed settlement, probably majority Serb, but there certainly is no -- there's no evidence that I know of that all the victims were Serbs or that none of the victims were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did a single member of the BH Army -- was a single member of the BH Army killed in this attack on Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not characterising the attacking force as the BH Army, I don't believe, but in any case I don't know what the casualties were on either side and can't attest to their nationality, although I believe the majority of the civilian casualties were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These killings of civilians and detentions, et cetera, civilians in Pofalici, is that a war crime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll leave that to others to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you include this in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned the Pofalici action in my Sarajevo report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 353 did you write: "Pejanovic is writing about a meeting towards the end of spring 1992 where prominent Serbs asked President Izetbegovic to stop mass detentions of Serbs in the Kosevo stadium." As for this mass detention of Serbs in Sarajevo, did you include that in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't read it, have you? There's a whole section on that incident in the report. I thought it was noteworthy and actually elaborated somewhat on what I had put in the book, as I discovered through investigating the periodical press that this basic account of Mr. Pejanovic is accurate and that further details were provided in a very candid story in "Oslobodjenje" right at the time that this occurred and certainly was a factor in dissuading the government from allowing this type of thing to take place again. So, yes, I did include it. I elaborated upon it and would put it in again if I were to write the report again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I know what you wrote. I just wanted a yes or no answer. Did you write about the fact that no one was ever held accountable for that crime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether anyone was held accountable for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You stated that: "... the fact that no one was ever held accountable for that crime." I've stated: "I don't know that to be the case."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on page 40 [No interpretation]: [In English] "In invoking fears of renewed anti-Serbian genocide, Bosnian Serb leaders relied upon the notion that the political foundation of the Ustasha regime from 1941 to 1945 was being constituted in the government of B&H 1991/1992. This premise reduced the complex alliance and events of the Second World War into a simple story of collaboration among Croats and Muslims against the Serbs." [Interpretation] The other day you confirmed that you did know that two SS Handzar Divisions had been established that consisted of Muslims. What I'm putting to you now is that they were the most cruel troops in Hitler's army. Did you think that that was an insignificant fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, being the most cruel troops in Hitler's army is a pretty low standard to set, and I do not believe that the -- this rather ragtag bunch would qualify to be the most cruel troops in Hitler's army, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you believe that -- or actually, is it correct that in your report Bosanska Krajina, on page 21, you said that German occupiers had established a special unit of Muslim recruits called the 13th Muslim SS Handzar Division, and you omitted to mention that in the beginnings of Republika Srpska or the origins of Republika Srpska. In this way, the Trial Chamber would have viewed matters in a different light. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you omit to refer to that in the origins of Republika Srpska, what you had written in Bosanska Krajina in the history of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows directly upon the sentences that you just read a minute ago. It's on page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that that was insignificant for the Trial Chamber to know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I can understand that you didn't read this recently, but you just asked me a direct question about whether it's there or not. I've told you it's there. It's on page 40. You can look at it yourself if you like. It's included. I think the sentence is somewhat different than I used in the Krajina report. I think it is a significant fact to be included in explaining why the Second World War and events, including the killings of many thousands of Serbs, did indeed play a role in political revival -- the political revivals in the 1990s. So there it is. I can't do anything more to draw your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. On page 281 of Sarajevo: The biography of a city. Did you write: "Propagandists underrated the Bosnian Muslims, claiming that they were Serbs of the Islamic faith who had betrayed the Serbian people and who had conspired to create Bosnia as a state of their own with Sarajevo as its capital. They were presented as sexually immoral and cowards, as second-rate citizens. Sarajevo was depicted as a land of darkness, suggesting that vestiges of Ottoman repression had poisoned city's life ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that by saying that the Muslims are the same thing as the Serbs that the Muslims are in that way being disparaged or underestimated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the context here or don't recall the context in which I made this statement, whether it was something out of the Second World War or the propaganda assault on the Muslims that came out of Belgrade in the late 1980s. I just don't recall exactly what I was saying. It would help if you'd buy the book, Dr. Karadzic, but failing that perhaps if I had a copy in front of me I could help more on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of one single Serbian propagandist who would have said this kind of thing about the Muslims or who had written or said something like this about the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I'll ask if I could see the context in which I said this and I think I can relate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Lord Owen said that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a civil war between and among the Serbs of the Orthodox faith, the Serbs of the Catholic faith, and the Serbs of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that to be one of many characterisations that he gave to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I -- they must run into the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that Serbs are proud of Serbs of the Muslim faith from Mehmet-Pasa Sokolovic to Mesa Selimovic and all others, and that all of these Muslims are genuine Serbs and that they're very popular among the Serb people and well liked too. I'm not referring to living persons. I'm only referring to those from the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that really relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may respond. Look at all the things that are being referred to here, what the Serbs are writing about the Muslims. What is relevant is to say that at a recent poll Mehmet-Paso Sokolovic was near the very top with Nikola Tesla, Prince Lazar, not to speak of Emir Kusturica, who is alive and well and Mesa Selimovic, who is a renowned writer in Serbia. No Serbs ever spoke of, in that way, of Muslims. So that is why it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
