utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 340 about this book about Sarajevo did you write: "Undeterred by a lack of weapons, the units of Bosnia-Herzegovina launched tens of offensives during the war with the intention of breaking through the siege or repelling the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska from the most vulnerable parts of town. They never managed to breakthrough the siege, but they did take key positions in town and they extended the territory that was under their control, especially in the western neighbourhoods." Is that what you wrote on page 340?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that in your report, in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes. Certainly not in those words and same formulation, but the -- I think I've actually described some of the offensives launched by the ARBiH to break the siege and agreed whole-heartedly with the notion that the city was defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Davy Crockett and --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not from West Virginia. I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Robin Hood, would you call them bandits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. What is your next question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you call Serb fighters against the Turks, those who fought the Turks for 500 years, why did you call them bandits? You know that we are proud of these fighters and that there is epic poetry that speaks of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're using the word "hajduk" in some -- yes, I think that's a word that Serb nationalities and Serbs generally use with great pride to describe the -- what they were, bandits, and they were, you know, throughout various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina particularly eastern Herzegovina, there's a rich epic poetry about them that dates back to, probably, the battle of Kosovo or possibly even earlier. And I think that's -- this kind of mythology is true of most peoples -- the folk literature of peoples of south-east Europe and elsewhere in the world. So I don't see what's the problem. It seems to me a source of pride to Serbs and to non-Serbs. I don't agree that these people always fought the Turks. There were times where Serb fighters were fought in the Ottoman forces on behalf of the Ottoman Empire, as well as at times against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, those are vessels, but the "hajduk" are the pride of the Serbian people. If they do not correspond to Davy Crockett, who fought against an occupation, they would correspond to the French resistance movement. Would you call the French resistance movement banditry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's move on here. I think you are coming to a close, Mr. Karadzic. Ask your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Excellency, if we do not get more time and if you do not fully reject Mr. Donia's report, the Defence will consider this witness not to have been examined or cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, did you find justification for all actions of the SDA and to a lesser extent the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean did I identify their -- the reasons that they cited to undertake them? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you identify them and did you find justification for their sins, or rather, did you hold anything against them? Did you establish any breaches on their part? Did you establish anything that they did that contributed to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think I did, yes. I've been -- we've just been talking about a number of things that I wrote about, some of them in the book, some of them in the paper, some of them in both, which are clearly acts that are -- were unhelpful in terms of the cause of war or the conduct of war. And I don't shrink from that in the least. I think they must be a part of the narrative that we as historians prepare about the war. Frankly, I have to say I think that some of the documents that you've submitted to me and to other witnesses will contribute to making that narrative more -- richer. So when I talk about specific events, certainly I've described the actions associated with the treatment of Serbs in Sarajevo in very stark terms, I believe, probably didn't identify all of them, but in general I've made the point that Serbs, indeed, were suffering double jeopardy in the course of the siege. They were being bombarded by you from the hills and they were being discriminated against and some cases imprisoned and killed by paramilitary forces within the city which were either Croat or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't identify anything else apart from that. Is there a contribution to our suffering, ours and theirs during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are -- I'm sorry, what are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that's all that you identified is their contribution to our suffering? You didn't find anything else to have been their sin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's not -- I don't believe that's true, no. I went into some of these incidents in detail, but as a general rule noted that the various parties were hard-lined in their pursuit of specific interests and that contributed to the outbreak of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we expect to get that from you, specified in some way, as you specified all the things that you hold against the Serbs? After having seen what you did and heard what you did from me and from other witnesses, do you intend to expand your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Donia. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again that's comment and accusations against Dr. Donia, albeit this time in a much more quiet tone of voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Donia is capable of dealing with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer I think is that I have addressed those issues in the report, I'm sure not to your satisfaction and I'm sure not in a way that portrayed this as a -- as the Serbs being lily-white pure and exclusive victims of aggressive hostile actions by the other sides. So I didn't address it the way, I'm sure, you want me to. But I believe the essential story is there, and I have no intention at this point to revise the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that the Croats had established first the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and then the Republic of Herceg-Bosna because of the Serbs. Are you saying that they voluntarily gave up on the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that to this day that is what they are seeking and that they are not giving up on their entity at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what Croats you're speaking of. There has been, indeed, ever since the formal abolition of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in 1998 some interest on the part of extreme nationalist Croats within the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to form a third entity. At times that movement has been very active and won widespread support and posed a considerable challenge to, let's say, the integrity of the Federation and the ten cantons that made it up. But I think for the most part it's been something that's been in the back of people's minds and they focused -- Croat nationalists in Bosnia have tended to focus their attentions on life in the individual cantons and also in the Assembly of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, now just yes or no. Did they continue to ask for their own entity in order to protect themselves from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said some of them do not -- are not seeking their own entity, and the reasons that those who are seeking their own entity are various. They are, I think, demanding a territorial unit that is the equivalent of the Republika Srpska and under the control of a single nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the entire activity of the SDA, did you identify actions that pre-eminently led to the outbreak of war? Can you mention some if you did identify any?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- you're not bringing me back to a point where I could name you how I identified these things. I did discuss the SDA's role at various points along the way, but my primary focus, of course, was on the SDS formation of the Serbian -- or the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, and the various activities that the SDS had undertaken. So it was not really the primary focal point of my report. I wasn't trying to present a kind of a billiard ball account. That's just the way I refer to these notions that if one group starts to move in one direction, it automatically evokes a response, a predetermined response from the other. I was rather trying to chronicle the development of the Republika Srpska and the main thinking that went into those people, including yourself who formed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that the Trial Chamber wouldn't benefit from knowing what the other two sides did?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much. I would certainly love to see someone write a report comparable to the one that I did on the formation of Republika Srpska and one on the behaviour of the various groups that were contending for influence and power in the area of Sarajevo using the documentation of all the other actors. It would be welcome to me. I'm not too sure how much use it would be to the Trial Chamber, but I have a feeling that it will fall to others, other than myself, to prepare those -- that type of narrative because the documentation is voluminous and it's a major undertaking. The reason I say that is the way in which the history of the Second World War has come to be understood really goes considerably to a historian, Professor Tomasevic, who wrote, in fact, of the war from the point of view of the three major actors. I'd love to see the same thing undertaken for the -- both the Sarajevo situation and Bosnia as a whole, but right now I don't see exactly who might step forward and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the Trial Chamber must work in the meantime and it won't have an overall picture. Can you tell the Trial Chamber of the sins committed by the Muslim part of the authorities because we were in the government too, a third of the government. What about the Muslim part of the government, the sins committed by them which led to war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I get the sense, Dr. Karadzic, that you're more than amply testifying to the -- what you consider the sins committed by the other sides. I don't know that I would use the word "sins," and I'm not sure we don't have a translation issue there. But as I say, that's a bit out of the purview of my report. I do try to bring it in, in terms of talking about the controversies, the contests that the SDS fought, and I do that both in the Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo report and also in the origins of the RS report. But I think that my job mainly is to illuminate the conduct and developments -- the conduct of the Bosnian Serb Leadership and the developments that led to the formation of the Republika Srpska in the case of the one report and the Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo in the other report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you understood and that the Trial Chamber will understand the acts of the Serb side without an overall comprehensive integral picture, yes or no? Is what you've done enough for the Trial Chamber to gain an impression of what actually happened over there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope it is enough to enable them to gain an impression, but it is, in a sense, designed to be a framework report. And I am sure the Trial Chamber will dig much deeper into events and the issue of the relative causes and contributions of various events to the principal issues at -- that are contested in the indictment. So I view this as just an introduction in no way comprehensive and not, in fact, intended to enter into the decisions, judgements, that the Trial Chamber will make regarding the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you include -- or rather, did you differentiate between what Serb actions were legal and lawful and those that were illegal and unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stipulate a single exculpatory circumstance as far as the Serbs were concerned -- mitigating circumstance as far as the Serbs were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the excerpts report is in fact a rich collection of statements by Serbs, explaining what they believed were the justifications for their actions, and in fact by SDS members and by yourself as president of the SDS. So I think that there's an awful lot of what you would, perhaps as the attorney for yourself, characterise as exculpatory evidence. I think we both agree that the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions provide an enormous amount of information about that very topic, and I would hope that it will indeed be weighed by the -- anybody seeking to make decisions about exactly the circumstances you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, the Serb positions and Serb words you subjected to your own characterisations and they don't look good in your interpretation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them do not. I think that the -- I haven't subjected -- in the excerpts report, I haven't subjected them to my own characterisations. I have subjected them to my own selection. And certainly you or anyone else can contest the selections that I made, and I would actually expect you to. But the excerpts report is designed to allow you and others to speak for yourselves in characterising the events and causes of the time. That is the whole spirit in which the excerpts report was prepared. It's why I, for example, in the chapter on regionalisation provide a whole series of quotations from people over time, SDS members, Serbs in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and yourself, about exactly what was going on with the municipal strategy or regionalisation at that time. I think you've correctly identified what the purpose and spirit of the excerpts report was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you list the Serb moves that were legitimate, legal, and justified from the elections to the outbreak of war? Can you enumerate them because that was not set out? Could you tell us what it was that the Serbs did with every reason and with every right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I -- you elicited from me previously, and as I spelled out in the preface to the report, my purpose in writing the reports was not to judge what was legal, constitutional, or justified; it was to describe as well as to identify causes. And I further believe that the quest using the constitution and laws to determine what was constitutional, legal, what was unconstitutional and illegal, is something of an exercise in futility because the mechanisms either were not there or were not used by the players at the time to determine what was indeed unconstitutional -- unconstitutional or illegal, constitutional or legal in the eyes of the appropriate courts or constitutions. So, no, I'm not going to do it now. I did not do it not report. I'm not trying to enter into those judgements of black/white, right/wrong. I'm trying to describe the course of events and account for the reasons that things developed the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then agree that the Trial Chamber should not take into account all your characterisations about events as contained in your report? Should they disregard them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confident that the Trial Chamber will take into account those matters which they deem to be relevant to their decisions. I have tried to, let's say, hit that target myself, but probably have opted on that -- in the direction of being more comprehensive, more descriptive, and more all-encompassing than they will ultimately determine to be within the field or within the world of relevant matters that they will assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you identify any action of the Muslim part of the authorities which led to war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking the same question but repeatedly in different forms. I have not made those kinds of moral judgements. They do enter the narrative in various ways, going way back to the elections and the -- their relationship to the outbreak of war. I haven't put a percentage on, I haven't attempted to do -- engage in a political science exercise of testing various hypotheses about things leading up to the cause of war. The situation really doesn't lend itself very well to that kind of inquiry in any case, but I believe I've tried to or I have tried to incorporate those events which directly impinged upon the ultimate outbreak of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's have yes or no answers, please. Did you show sufficient understanding for the Serbs concerns and fears?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given you, I think, far more than most people frankly want to read to try to capture what Serbs felt their concerns and fears were at the time. That's the essence of the or one -- certainly one central part of the excerpts report. And also figures in -- descriptively in my other two accounts. I personally think the question of fears is a really elusive one and difficult to, let's say, address empirically, although I think it is one that needs to be less a matter of sheer speculation than many people would assume. I think people make a lot of assumptions about what fears were on the basis of sort of an intuitive feeling. And in many cases they may be completely wrong about that. That's why I felt it was important to let Serb delegates to the Bosnian Serb Assembly speak for themselves, let you speak for yourself in the language of the time, expressing -- and I assume that in most cases you were sincerely voicing your viewpoint at that time about the concerns and fears that you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately we don't have the time to go through the Assembly and your selections from the Assembly, but I hope we can have a yes or no answer now. Is it correct that the Assembly exists so that through free discussion it can pass decisions, acts, documents, like the constitution, and so on. Does the Assembly exist in order to engender various acts and documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's its primary purpose, but it also exists to provide a venue in which people can express widely differing viewpoints, issue criticisms of the government, allow for delegates' questions, allow for reports from the various ministers to the Assembly, and to issue guide-lines for behaviour of the government leaders, including yourself, or others, sometimes rubber-stamping them, other times genuinely molding them after a pretty free and open debate. So I think it's fair to say that you've characterised the purpose of the Assembly in a way that I would agree with. I'd probably choose to make it a little bit broader and or comprehensive, at least as I observed the function of the Assembly through these, I think, 63 sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in the Assembly -- Republika Srpska Assembly documents, did you ever come across any extremist stands by the deputies mirrored and reflected in the documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that that was unlawful; right? Well, tell us, go ahead, tell us, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I find a growing extremism in the characterisation of claims to Serb lands. That was something that I think began with the, at least, assumption that Serb land consisted of the land in those municipalities in which the Serbs held an absolute majority. But then in the early, say, late winter of 1992, in particular at the -- I believe it was the 11th Session, you kind of indicated that there was a quiet deal made with one of the other sides, which certainly had to be the Croats, that you agreed that land would be claimed by any group that held either an absolute or a relative majority in the municipality. And then very shortly thereafter, that definition was broadened to include the definition of Serb land as anywhere where the plebiscite of November 9th and 10th had been held. Then it was further broadened by the provision, which eventually made it into the constitution, that Serb land also included anywhere that Serbs had been the victims of genocide in the Second World War. And finally you get to the era of the formalised six strategic goals and see at the 17th Session that Serb land is defined by a recommendation to the Assembly presented by Mr. Koljevic that was based on the rivers specified in the strategic goals, plus a series of mountaintops, rivers, river valleys, and cities which seemed to have no relationship to the distribution of peoples in these areas. And I think that -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly functioned as the venue in which these increasingly expansive claims became more extreme. Yes, that's one example I would say of an extremist stands that was deputy -- mirrored by the deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you found a law, a law, or some other document passed by the Assembly which was unlawful. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't your question, Dr. Karadzic. I answered your question and you can go back and see it. You're asking me if -- now you're asking me if I found a law that was unlawful; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a logical impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, couldn't some of our laws be in contravention to international law, for example?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever come across such a law or any other document? When I say "act," I mean document produced by the Assembly, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never held any resolution or the -- any resolution, law, proposal, or anything in the Assembly up against that standard. I wouldn't be qualified to judge it even if I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you described to us and said that the Christian majority made up of the Serbs and Croats did not have the right to hold consultations and agreements on a possible resistance to the -- an Islamic republic. But you're not challenging the right when that majority was composed of Muslims and Croats, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Just to understand your question: Am I challenging the right of the majority to consult and reach agreements? No. I noted that the agreement that was being pursued between the HDZ and the SDS included -- basically it was being made by -- under the auspices of the president of another neighbouring republic which had become an independent state and that the -- when that agreement was made in Grac on May 6th, 1992, that you were notified by the European Community that such a law or such an agreement was contrary to the principles that had been established for the Conference of the former Yugoslavia of the European Community. I think that's a somewhat different issue -- that we were really talking about two different times in the first place, and once the internationalisation of this occurred under the European Community there were clearly different principles in play than existed at the time of the Assembly session on October 14/15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, taking into account the fact that any negotiation involves giving up on some things, do you agree that many of our statements, at the beginning of a process, were naturally more extreme more tactical reasons, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you happen to notice or do you accept the fact that some of our statements had as their goal to dissuade the SDA or the HDZ from undertaking some of their actions, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept the fact that some of the statements had as their goal or your goal to dissuade the SDA or the HDZ from -- to dissuade, defer them from undertaking some of their actions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the Islamic Declaration is by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At last. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Islamic Declaration, if it were to be put into practice, does it envisage further modernisation of life in Bosnia and the convergence of the three national communities or entities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like you to show me where it refers to Bosnia in the Islamic Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Every Islamic society is mentioned, every country in which Islamic is sufficiently strong to carry out a revolution and to topple the old order and establish a new one on Islamic foundations. Let me help you out here. Do you remember how Izetbegovic defended himself in 1983 before the court in Sarajevo? And he said that it didn't refer to Yugoslavia because in Yugoslavia only 19 per cent of the population were Muslims, and it doesn't refer to Bosnia either because 39 per cent of the population in Bosnia were Muslims. So it depended on the numbers, not on the fact that it was Bosnia or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not too sure exactly what the question is, but at this point I think you've just acknowledged that neither Bosnia nor Yugoslavia is referenced at all in the Islamic Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All territories inhabited by Muslims are mentioned. Now, taking the Islamic Declaration again, does it envisage the Muslimisation of the community; first of all, the Muslims and then the whole community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your statement is false. It does not reference all territories inhabited by Muslims. He probably refers to two to three dozen different states, but he doesn't refer to Yugoslavia which has a -- had then, has now -- or if you look at the former Yugoslavia, a substantial Muslim population. So your -- the premise of your question is false. The Islamic Declaration is basically the writings of a Islamic believer who is seeking to find a middle way between the two trends in Islam at that time which he felt were unwise. And one was the movement toward a modern secular state, the model of which he found in Pakistan. And the other direction that he deplored was the -- what we would probably characterise today as the fundamentalist direction, in which the state functions are all determined by Islamic law. And he tried to weave a -- sort of a middle ground between these, remembering that this was written just after the 1967 Middle Eastern war in which the Islamic countries of the Middle East had suffered substantial defeats. And this had set off a crisis, really, among Islamic thinkers about whether they should try to modernise their societies to become militarily more effective or whether they should return to a much more, let's say, pietistic reliance on Islamic law. Now, it's just helpful to look at what his statements are in the light of that effort to determine or to lay out a middle path between those two, what he considers, extreme options. And I would agree that he makes statements in there in which he argues that Muslims should take over a state if they reach a certain threshold of the population. There -- as you read through it, I think you barely notice them at first, but, of course, they have been highlighted, dragged out many, many times, put on the internet and highlighted by Izetbegovic's critics from people like you to Zulfikarpasic, and a whole bunch of other people to argue that he was an Islamic fundamentalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court 1D1434.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you, Mr. Donia, I have been given permission, what are your earnings at this Tribunal per hour? How much money have you earned during your 15 testimonies here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, yes. I believe you were in the United States in the mid-1970s, and if you watched television there was a programme on featuring James Garner, it was the Rockford Files. And if you recall in the early 1970s, James Rockford, who was a private detective was paid $200 a day plus expenses. That's what I'm paid. Those are days that I spend testifying, preparing for testimony, and preparing the reports that I have submitted to you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you anti-Serb, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you joined this action against the Serbs, Noel Malcolm, Marko Attila, then Branka Magas, Tom Gallagher, Smajo Cekic, Jasmin Jahic, did you sign this letter that you see before you, this letter, this open letter to the presidents of the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and to the Republic of Serbia to do everything possible to accuse Serbia of genocide?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, indeed, recall signing this some -- several years ago. There was a time when I actually was not certain that I had signed it, but I do now have an active recollection of signing it. I don't consider the document to be anti-Serb whatsoever. I think it is designed to or it is intended to be a direct critique of the refusal of the ICJ to subpoena the records of the Supreme Defence Council. I still believe today that that was a grave mistake, still hold that position, and was willing to go along with this group of people, most of who I know well and share at least some views with, but some with whom I have some pretty sharp disagreements in this particular letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you did agree on this anti-Serb action. Is this activism? Is this political activism, Mr. Donia? Or is this a scholarly effort?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I reject your characterisation of the action as anti-Serb. I think in fact it's probably something that if it were done would be -- that is, if our critique here would be followed would be a pro-Serb action because I think it would contribute to a more healthy environment in Serbia and a kind of a historical reckoning with the realities of the things that the Milosevic regime undertook in the course of 1990 to 1996, 1999 even. So, you know, I think the -- I don't know whether I would characterise it either as political or scholarly. It is a protest letter directed to a particular audience. As such, I think you could say, yes, it has a political purpose, to influence behaviour, hopefully to urge the ICJ or some other body to release in full the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council. But it's something that was really done at the same time in the interest of scholarship because I think the scholarship will be better and richer if the full contents of those minutes are put in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you think that you, as an expert and witness, should write to the President of this Tribunal and to take a position? Because this is, inter alia, sent to the President of this Tribunal too.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't see -- I see no inherent ban on my participating in an expression of such a view and in an open letter to the President of the Tribunal, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic, are you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in how many more minutes I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you are almost finished, but how many more minutes do you like to have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat the position of this Defence, namely, that this witness touched upon so many topics in a way that really calls for clarification. It is a fact that this paper is one of the basic foundations of the indictment. We asked for those 40 hours, didn't we? I would like to say on behalf of the Defence and on behalf of the accused that if these findings are not rejected, we will need -- I mean, if we don't work longer now, if we don't get more time now, we are going to suggest to bring Donia -- Dr. Donia back once again in order to clarify certain matters that we will not be able to clarify with others. Of course I would like to have his papers rejected because they are partial, unprofessional, political, and we believe that this is no expertise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, be practical. You have had so far almost 21 hours for your cross-examination. Let me come to Ms. Edgerton first. How long would you need for your re-direct? There are some administrative matters at the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: About half an hour I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Half an hour. We'll have a break for 25 minutes now and then you will have 15 minutes to conclude your cross-examination -- 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I was asked to clarify the meaning of 55 minutes which appears in the transcript. It should read 25 minutes, the length of the break. Mr. Karadzic, you have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you to admit 1D1434, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The English version of that letter that I see in e-court isn't complete, so perhaps it could be marked for identification subject to the entire English document being uploaded. I miss in the English version several pages of signatories to the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was only of two pages, so -- but there should be more.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbo-Croatian version is much longer actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. I don't think there's problem in getting those translations. Yes. For completeness we'll mark it for identification, pending we'll get the full translation. The original should be in English I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So perhaps we could have the full original uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that understanding, we'll just mark it -- we'll just admit it in its entirety, but the understanding is that we'll have the full document. That's D340?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence is also interested in having all the names there because you're not going to find a single document with that many anti-Serbs in one place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's an unnecessary comment, Mr. Karadzic, and unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to say something, Excellencies. What is left for us? The entire activity of the Assembly, the Prosecution and the expert cannot find a single Assembly document that went against the law, either domestic law or international law. So many speeches, sentences, parts of speeches were selected and used against us that it requires a great deal of work to be done in order to bring things into context and view matters in their entirety. Also, we haven't dealt with municipalities at all. We haven't done anything in relation to the Siege of Sarajevo. Believe me, our 40 hours was a conservative estimate. I don't think it would be useful for me to open any of these subjects now that we could not deal with properly. So I am giving this time back as a present. I know it's unnecessary for me to say this but I can't resist. There wasn't even any need to have any re-direct because Mr. Donia handled that on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you need that 15 minutes at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is pointless for me to raise any subjects without dealing them properly -- actually, I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know that Rajlovac was a municipality before it was included in Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I so reported in my report on the Sarajevo siege, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Rajlovac there was an important factory called Orao for the overhaul of aircraft engines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that factory and its revenues was the reason to include Rajlovac and Novi Grad, and that the revenues went to the municipality of Novi Grad and not to Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you trust the people who said since we've been abolished we have no schools, we have no sports centres, life has ground to a halt, why didn't you believe people that their revenues went to the municipality of Novi Grad and that they became impoverished in terms of their social institutions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I noted in my report that the nature of the complaints from people who proposed to separate Rajlovac from Novi Grad changed very much over time. It first -- and these apparently were complaints prepared with some consultation or advice from SDS members. The complaints began, as you've said here, that they had insufficient schools, sports centres, roads, inadequate communication between villages, and these general complaints that one often finds in rural areas about underdevelopment vis-a-vis the urban centre. However, when it came time to actually form the Rajlovac municipality, the argument completely switched and the applicants said: We can become our own municipality of Rajlovac because we have all the characteristics of modern urban life. We have lots of schools, we have sufficient roads, we have a well educated population, we have an economic base. So all the things that it -- these applicants had started out with in, I believe, early or sometime in summer of 1991 were completely reversed with the arrival of February 1992. So which one is to be believed? I mean, I think the -- we have to take both of them seriously, but I think they reflect the changing thinking of the SDS leaders and others who were promoting a separate Rajlovac and note that again the simple argument that we're promoting regionalisation or a new municipality strictly for economic reasons is probably -- probably not the sole reason that's being brought into play.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D1384.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know what "papak" means in our Sarajevo slang? "Papak" as you know is a trotter, that is to say the foot of a sheep, cow, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the term kind of suggests a peasant of rural, uneducated, unskilled person, whereas the opposite term, "raja" refers more to the urban, more sophisticated, more-comfortable-in-an-urban-environment type of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the original meaning of the word "raja" is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Raja" I think was a term for the sort of common people in the Ottoman period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Common people, non-Turkish, non-Ottoman, that is to say for slaves, Serbs. Mr. Donia, on page 32 you said that: [In English] "The proclamation revealed that peasant nostalgia has expressed for a bucolic rural life had been overtaken by the SDS campaign to acquire the many resources of Sarajevo urbanised Western approach." [Interpretation] Bucolic is "papak" and someone had suggested that to you, some of your informers from Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I deliberately stayed away from the "papak" "raja" dichotomy because it does mean different things to different people, and it did, in fact, become entwined in the political struggles of the early 1990s, but I didn't want to use it because it has clear, let's say, value connotations that I didn't particularly think were appropriate for the phenomenon I was examining. Bucolic to me means both rural and peaceful, tranquil, so I find this phenomenon of sort of people who have been let's say caught up in or incorporated into an urban area, but retain much of their -- or are struggling to retain their rural lifestyle, that's actually a very widespread, common phenomenon in the course of these huge urbanisation drives of the 20th century, and not just in Europe but in many different societies, including the US. So I was trying to avoid a value judgement here, and in fact describing this peasant nostalgia movement as authentic. I mean, it may not have a valid basis in terms of the economic arguments in all cases, but it nevertheless is something that's understandable for people in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were wondering who was right, those who said we have nothing and those who said we have everything. Both are right. If a municipality has its own revenue, then they have everything; and if somebody else uses their revenue, then they have nothing; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think you said it right the first time. They are both right. They are coming at the problem from two very different, let's say, interests. In the first instance trying to, let's say, they're trying to recover a sense of their own, let's say, rural tranquility by disparaging the lack of facilities and resources and then when they actually want to argue that they are -- can be self-sufficient, then they turn around and see, yes, we have all this stuff and we have a pretty educated population, we have the potential to do much more. So we believe that we qualify for this position. I don't believe that in the long run either one of those arguments really was -- I believe that they were employed by the SDS to promote the separation that they were seeking to do because the outcome of that was a Rajlovac that was compact territorially, included some important strategic resources, military resources, including the Orao factory, and therefore was in accord with the general SDS campaign to re-order the municipalities in the Western approaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, these people say that that is precisely why they were abolished as a municipality, so that the Serb municipality would not develop. Look at the last paragraph. You know our language and here it says "trump cards in the economy": "Economic potentials are the greatest trump cards of our municipality. The military institute of Orao is the leading work organisation there. Our giant here from Rajlovac and our pride. The distribution centre of Rajlovac is also a very strong company. The former seat of the UPI ..." and so on and so forth. Are you familiar with a socialist economy where all revenues go to the municipality and nothing is left to the local community, they only get something if the municipality hands something out? Do you know of that method that is the municipality that gathers all revenues?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, can we look at this document, I assume this to be "Srpsko Oslobodjenje"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it's no good if it's "Srpsko Oslobodjenje"? The man is saying this. It doesn't matter what newspaper it is. This is what the man is saying, the top person from Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would completely disagree that it doesn't make any difference what newspaper it is. "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" was founded precisely as a rival and parallel newspaper to the "Oslobodjenje" newspaper that was published in Sarajevo. As such, it had a very specific political agenda which was to champion the cause of Serbian Sarajevo and much of its content was, in fact, devoted to that. I do read Serbian Cyrillic, but I have to say I can't read this other than make out a few words. I, you know, find it unsurprising that "Srpsko Oslobodjenje" is trumpeting this cause. I guess I find it a little bit surprising that they're still beating that horse in I think it's 1994 is the date of this thing because it had long since been kind of established as an article of faith in the SDS organisation of Sarajevo that Rajlovac was separate. It doesn't surprise me, though, that this case is being made in this newspaper with the quotations from Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I omit to inform you that this is not a quotation. This is an interview with the president of one of Sarajevo's municipalities. Is this an interview with Mr. Bozic or not? Just say yes or no. We don't need more than that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't make out enough here to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the questions in italics and can you see the answers in whatever print this may be, whatever font? The questions are in italics and the answers are given in this regular type of print?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer that. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, Dr. Donia has said two times now he can't read it. So I would suggest the question's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Final try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've read it. I have read it. Economic potentials are our greatest trump card, and he mentions the companies on account of which they should keep the revenues rather than sending them to the Muslim municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else, Mr. Donia. Do you know that Pale was also an independent municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not independent, no. It was a separate municipality, one of the ten municipalities of the city of Sarajevo as of 1991, and declared its separation from the city of Sarajevo in May of 1991. As I reported in my report -- cited in my report, it really was the first municipality to declare its break-away from Sarajevo. It was a municipality in which the population was about 68 per cent Serb. The SDS won an absolute majority in its Municipal Assembly, and therefore took power in January of 1991. And it proceeded then to consolidate power further all the way up until it was basically ethnically cleansed in -- by the 6th of July, 1992. So it's a separate municipality, had a great deal of authority. As every municipality was a socio-economic entity and I think one of your favourite places to hold your headquarters and meetings and to live. I think it was, in a sense, your home in Sarajevo in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A few things that are inaccurate. However, one question: Are you denying that beforehand Pale was a separate municipality, out of town? And since my last question, do you know that Jahorina as an Olympic mountain is in Pale, and that is why Pale was included into Sarajevo and that was also the reason why Pale separated because they had this revenue of their own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've explained how that all happened, with the decision in 1976 to pursue this economic development plan, which included the inclusion of four new municipalities in 1977, one of which was Pale, and at the same time to develop both industry and service -- the service economy in these, what I call, peripheral municipalities, including Pale. Pale, of course, was the great beneficiary of the development of facilities in advance of the Olympic games of 1984 and probably received more investment from the city of Sarajevo in that period, from 1977 to, say, 1984, probably received more investment than any other single municipality. So the -- although there were these people who viewed Pale as a somehow backward impoverished municipality, in fact it had been a huge beneficiary of the economic resources of the city -- capital that was available to the city to develop the facilities for the Olympic games. And it was comparably very easy for Pale to simply draw a line and say, We're going to draw a line and say, We're going to generate this revenue here, not forward it to the headquarters of the companies that had made the investments in the first place in Sarajevo, call it the enterprises that had made those investments, and declare its separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document? I'd still like to request 19 more hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the only evidence we have on the content of that document comes from the mouth of Dr. Karadzic himself, so I would object to that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Agreed. We'll not admit this document. You'll have another opportunity to lead this evidence. Before Ms. Edgerton start your re-direct, Judge Baird has some questions for Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you have been testifying for some time, so I have no intention of prolonging your stay here, but there are just two small matters on which I should like some clarification. Now, I propose to give a brief summary of the surrounding evidence. First of all, to help you to refresh your memory, and, at the same time, to put the question in some perspective. Now, I want to refer, first of all, to the proceedings of the 2nd of June, and Ms. Edgerton this is -- Dr. Karadzic, this is at page 3270, 3270, lines 10 to 14. Now, in reference to a video-clip in which Eagleburger made certain comments, Dr. Karadzic asked you: "So do you see that this was a purely political issue, a domestic, political issue related to the elections and that Mr. Eagleburger is aware of the fact that it was unlawful?" And you replied: "No. I would not concur that what you just showed me establishes that. He -- this is first of all -- these are carefully selected excerpts from statements by, as I indicated, many different public figures in the crisis, which are deliberately selected apparently in this video to make a particular point, and that means it is really, I think, a Serb propaganda film ." Now, this was part of your answer. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now I turn to page 3271, Ms. Edgerton, Dr. Karadzic, lines 3 to 9, and Dr. Karadzic then referred you to a video-clip that had been shown a short while before. This is page 3269, lines 3 to 14, of James Baker making certain comments. And he stated: "But James Baker did say it was unlawful because it was one-sided and violent. Breaking up a country and its borders that had been guaranteed by the Helsinki Final Act and the constitutions of the republic and the constitution of the SFRY." And he then asked you: "So did Baker not confirm here that it had been illegal? So is that Serb propaganda?" Now, this was a compound question and you answered the first component. You stated: "He held that opinion." But I think it must have slipped you to answer the second component, and so can you now tell us whether you would characterise the Baker video-clip in the same manner as you characterised the Eagleburger video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I have is these were two American secretaries of state. I think Baker followed Eagleburger, and the time of these pronouncement isn't clear in the film or it wasn't clear to me anyway. I have reviewed the entire film, I've seen the entire film --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and characterised it, and I think I would still characterise it as a Serbian propaganda film. It is highly selective. I don't dispute the accuracy of the words that were said by the public figures that are interviewed, only that they may have been taken out of context and in many cases were not attached to a particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: That is both the Eagleburger clip and the Baker clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. I see, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as you know, US policy was kind of shifting in this period. It started out being very strongly pro-Yugoslav/unified Yugoslav, and then shifted in the course of 1991, the latter half of 1991, to much more sympathetic position to the withdrawal of the -- or the separation of Slovenia and Croatia from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Now, I have -- I take you now to the proceedings of the 7th of June, and, Ms. Edgerton, Dr. Karadzic, this is at page 3428, lines 13 to 15; and page 3429, lines 1 to 3. Now, Dr. Karadzic asked you, Dr. Donia, whether you agreed that towards the end of August Izetbegovic fully called off the agreement, the Serb/Muslim agreement, and you replied in the affirmative. And if I might summarise, you stated that he became concerned about the good faith of particularly Milosevic's commitments that he had expressed Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic6 c 18.23.30 and was concerned about the efforts that Dr. Karadzic and Milosevic were taking to undermine his personal position politically at that time. So you said yes, he did walk away from it very clearly in the latter part of August. Now, Dr. Karadzic then sought to correct you. He said that it was not because of that, it was because he did not want to remain in Yugoslavia if it were to be reduced by no longer including Slovenia and Croatia. He then asked whether you agreed that he said he did not want to stay in a Yugoslavia where Serbs would constitute a majority. And you replied: Yes, I think his position at that time and somewhat before it and after it can be characterised as wanting to have Bosnia-Herzegovina have an equal position with the other republics vis-a-vis Yugoslavia. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Why then did he walk away from the agreement? For the second reason or for both reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think for both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: For both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I can clarify a bit about the efforts to undermine him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once the initial momentum for this agreement between the MBO and the SDS was lost and it started to get more complicated, there was an effort on the part of Mr. Milosevic, with the knowledge and co-operation of Dr. Karadzic, to make a representation at the opening session of the European Community talks on Yugoslavia that Bosnia had already decided it wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. And they did this by convening a group of presidents of the Assemblies of the republics of Yugoslavia. So the meeting was attended by the president of the Assembly of Montenegro and the president of the Assembly of Serbia. I believe Macedonia too. But in any case, Mr. Krajisnik attended as a represent of Bosnia, and that meeting resulted in a declaration. That declaration then was presented at the first EC -- first opening session of the EC meeting, and Milosevic contended that Krajisnik was authorised to speak on behalf of Bosnia, saying that they had reached this agreement. Now, this was clearly a dubious representation, to take the president of the Assembly and submit that his adherence to this would then mean that all of Bosnia was obligated to stay in the Yugoslav Federation. And it was meant to embarrass Izetbegovic, as we know from a couple of intercepts from around this time, and indeed it did. The European Community leaders didn't really buy this at all, but nevertheless it was run past them, and it was a clear effort to undermine Izetbegovic in the eyes of the international negotiators. That's what I mean by the loss of trust or confidence and the suspicions that developed about Milosevic's intentions. On the other hand, I also cite this other reason, which was the firm position that there should be this parity in the relationship of various republic leaders to the Federation. That was inherent in Izetbegovic's and Tupurkovski's proposal of June of 1991 which was eventually embraced by the presidents of all six republics on June 6th and reiterated on June 12th amongst the three presidents. And that policy carried consistently through until the Assembly session of October 14/15, when it then didn't change. So I think that on both grounds Izetbegovic was uncomfortable about this whole agreement and decided to opt out of it. I kind of wish he hadn't, but that was what was going on. And as far as I can discern, that is what was driving his decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much indeed, Dr. Donia, for that. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, today at page 5, lines 13 to 24, and page 6, lines 4 to 5, of this transcript, you referred to an agreement that Mr. Koljevic sought with President Tudjman in Zagreb on the 8th of January just before the actual proclamation of the state in which the two of them talked, and then there's some overlapping speakers, and then you continue, the division of Bosnia and the formation of new municipality lines, again overlapping speakers, to use the coercive powers of the state to force the human division in Bosnia as well. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 00987, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we wait for both versions, could I -- Ah, we have both versions then. Dr. Donia, we have before us minutes of a meeting between the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Tudjman, and his associates with members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Professor Nikola Koljevic and Mr. Franjo Boras held in Zagreb on 8 January 1992. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this document or does this document have any relation to the meeting you referred to in your testimony earlier today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, in fact, a meeting I was referring to. It was in President Tudjman's office. He arrives somewhat late in the meeting and is represented by number of his most senior advisors up until the point that he arrives. And Professor Koljevic and -- who's the -- of course the -- one of the two Serb members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr. Boras, who was one of the Croat representatives on -- presidents on the Presidency of Bosnia travelled to Zagreb together to attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to e-court page 13, pages 13 and 14 in the English version. Ah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to the top of the page where we see Franjo Boras speak, Dr. Donia. And he says: "We have some maps which was drawn up now after the population census on the basis of which, as you can see, that is the part that is primarily Croatian and that is the part which is very compact and the easiest -- eastern Herzegovina is the easiest." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, he continues in this paragraph on the subject of a reorganisation of municipalities, and then further in the page Dr. Koljevic enters the discussion, referring to the homogeneity of certain areas. Have you seen these passages before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in Dr. Koljevic's discussion, he talks about the notion at I think three lines down after his name appears to the effect that: "It would be a good idea to establish an agency which would regulate the exchange of property and to raise this to a civilised level." And continues further: "It is not so impossible to divide Bosnia." Do you see these passages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do these passages by Dr. Koljevic, and we could go over to page 14 in English, and Dr. Boras have any relation to the coercive powers of the state to enforce the human division in Bosnia that you referred to earlier today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I noted the use of government agencies to issue permits and over time to use the various powers of the state to -- permitting being one of them, to actually effect a human separation following the -- in this proposal, following the redrawing of municipal boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be tendered, please, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P986.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, referring to the transcript of the 8th of June, so a couple of days ago, page 3499, lines 9 to 10, you had a discussion with Dr. Karadzic about an intercept between he and one Gojko Djogo. And Dr. Karadzic said to you: "I'm saying to everybody that regardless of what I would accept, there would be chaos, a chaos would ensue in Bosnia-Herzegovina in two hours. Do you think that I could control 2 million Serbs who would rebel against this attempt to take them back to Turkish times?" And your response was: "Yes, I do believe you had sufficient control of the SDS and the broader Serb followers of the party to do that." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask for 65 ter 30722 to be brought up, please, that's a transcript of an intercepted conversation between one Mr. Kupresanin and General Kukanjac on -- in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, you noted in your testimony as well, this -- on page 3403, lines 10 to 12 that Mr. Kupresanin was the person who was elected president of the community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina on 25 April 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And similarly, you identified at page 3138, lines 16 to 19, General Kukanjac as the JNA commander of the military district centre in Sarajevo which covered essentially all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the intercept transcript is on the screen in front of us. Before I ask you further questions, could I ask: Are you familiar with this intercept? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 then of the English and I think it's the same in the B/C/S version. The B/C/S version should be a little bit smaller so that we can scroll down in the B/C/S version. It might be page 3. Uh-huh. It should be page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, page 2, halfway down the page approximately, there's a statement by Mr. Kupresanin in response to a comment by General Kukanjac and he says: "Well, we must and now we are waiting for Karadzic to return from Europe ..." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you read the rest of the passage for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, we must and now we are waiting for Karadzic to return from Europe and tell us what we are to do next. I personally think, general, that I won't do anything until he returns, when he comes whatever he tells us we will do. He is now for us the supreme commander and we have no other commander. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one side and the Serb people in the situation they are in on the other. We have our commander, it is that man, we must obey him, you understand us, we understand you."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is this passage consistent with your articulated position of Dr. Karadzic's control over the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If perhaps I could just elaborate a little bit the recent history prior to this intercept. We've spoken about this persistent challenge to Karadzic's leadership from the Bosnian Krajina area, and this -- that challenge last surfaced at the time that the constitution of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted in late February of 1992. And at that time there was a real effort to declare the Bosnian Krajina a separate republic, separate from the one that Dr. Karadzic was leading. And the next day after that constitution was approved, Dr. Karadzic made a trip to Banja Luka and spent the entire day meeting with the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and a couple of different groups of officials and successfully persuaded all of them, persuaded a few of them to actually walk out of the meeting, and the rest of them to embrace the constitution that had been passed in Sarajevo the previous day. I regard that as a kind of signal event in establishing the unity of the SDS, and it never really after that crumbled again. It kind of was the crowning event in bringing the Bosnian Krajina back into the -- really, the centre of the SDS and establishing Dr. Karadzic's leadership of the entire party.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be -- please be marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done -- yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? What this is about is the moment when --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Yugoslavia left us to fend for ourselves, and I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- would like the date to be established there. There's no date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be -- that can be done, yes. Can we see the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The date that the Prosecution has was April 1992, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see. April 1992. But we don't have the date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not good enough for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for you to comment, Mr. Karadzic. This will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As MFI P987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Is there no way the date of this can be absolutely established beyond any doubt?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Possibly, but it would take me to make some inquiries overnight and we could advise the Chamber at the next sitting. I just need to check some additional documentation that isn't immediately available to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Next, Dr. Donia, on June -- referring to the transcript of June 9, and I have in my notes the old page citation. My apologies. Page 60, lines 12 to 16. You were asked by Dr. Karadzic: "Have you come across a single document stating that this document," in reference to Variant A and B, "was discussed and adopted by organs of the Serbian Democratic Party?" And your response was: "A lot of documentary evidence that it was forwarded to local municipal boards by the main board and this from a variety of different municipalities." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask to see P970, please, an excerpt from a transcript of the 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, dated 15/16 April 1995, page 316 in the English and page 278 in the B/C/S. And it's an excerpt from a speech by Dr. Karadzic. Now, in the English page 316, if we could go nine lines down from the top of the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the sentence, Dr. Donia, in the ninth line that reads: "At the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, municipal boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B variants. In the B variant where we were in the minority - 20 per cent, 15 per cent - we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit, no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander." Do you see the passage I've just read, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this passage - and for the record that's referred to in Dr. Donia's Sarajevo report at footnotes 114 and 149 - is this passage an excerpt from the transcript of the 50th Session one of those documents which you've referred to showing the adoption of Variant A and B by municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on. On 9 June at page 3614, lines 23 to 25; and 3615, lines 1 to 7, you were asked by Dr. Karadzic what the Serbs were doing at the time, exclusively political moves they were making, now did you know what the other side was doing and forcing the Serbs to react and take political steps, they were provoking the Serb side?" Your answer was: "I don't share the premise of your question that the Serbs at the time were only doing political moves. I think that the SDS was busy arming its people and becoming essentially a paramilitary unit unto itself and all sorts of things were going on to make sure that the SDS had the co-operation and support of the JNA in pursuing whatever course it might choose to take after the fall of 1991." Do you remember that question and that answer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Further, at page 3615, lines 19 to 25; and 3616, line 1, asked about -- asked by Dr. Karadzic whether you wanted to say that in September 1991 the Serbian Democratic Party was in favour of the disintegration of Yugoslavia and that the JNA served it apart from the fact that the SDS supported the JNA, you responded: "I did not make that statement and don't believe that that was the case. I think the coming together of the SDS and the JNA, or what really proved to be a very close working alliance, was just getting started in the early couple of weeks of September 1991, and they grew closer but somewhat erratically in the months of that. There clearly were some efforts on the part of the JNA to distribute arms to members of the SDS prior to that, but in terms of the kind of top-level co-operative relationship that started about this same time." Now, with this same document in front of us, I would like to just - if I could have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours - in the English version page 316 just below the halfway mark, underneath -- two lines underneath where you see the words "20 per cent" and "15 per cent," and in the B/C/S it's about 19 lines up from the bottom of the page, I'd like to direct you to the same speech by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for record, it's page 145 of 376.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's a confusing number that appears on the bottom of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see, Dr. Donia, the passage that -- I'm sorry, could we go back to page 316, please, e-court page 316?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No need. Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, we see here a passage that begins: "The war began and the JNA helped as much as it could here and there ..." And I note we also find this in part in your excerpts report at paragraph 235. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
