utterances.text: All right. Is this passage which says, among other things, distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA, a manifestation of that top-level co-operative relationship you described between the SDS and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could remove that document and go to P979, please. And P979 dated 20 March 1992 is a report from the command of the Yugoslav People's Army 2nd Military District, conclusions of the evaluation of the situation on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Military District. Are you familiar with this document, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it represents.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report by General Kukanjac regarding the -- it gets quite specific about the distribution of the various arms in the possession of the JNA into the hands of local SDS authorities. Subsequent pages give both some specifics of places where those were distributed to and times they were distributed, as well as an annex which includes the number of forces in each municipality that are available to the JNA to fight whatever war may be impending.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard, if we could go to page 6 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, please. Dr. Donia, in paragraph 5(f), I note we see reference to the distribution of weapons of 5.000 -- pardon me, 51.900 weapons by the JNA and 17.298 by the SDS. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this passage in the document as a whole also reflective of the co-operative relationship you've described?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects the, by this time, very close operational co-operation between the SDS and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll move on to - your indulgence for a moment - the transcript from June 9th, page 3600 lines 1 to 11, first of all, and there, Dr. Donia, in the context of a discussion regarding the Variant A and B document, you were asked a question, and the question was: "And do you know that in practically all municipalities there were negotiations to the effect that each community would establish its own municipality, in Sanski Most, for instance, in Vlasenica, and Bratunac. Actually, in Vlasenica negotiations to the effect that each community would establish its own municipality. Actually, in Vlasenica and Bratunac that had already been established," and so forth. Your answer was: "The only situations that I know of like that, and I would be open to knowing of other ones, would be -- pardon me, were those negotiations undertaken essentially at the point of a gun starting in early April 1992, usually with an ultimatum of some sort issued by the SDS just prior to the actual take-over and ethnic cleansing of a municipality." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, further at page 3608, lines 7 to 25, in the context of a discussion about D297, which was a handwritten document, you were asked your view as to whether a demographic imbalance in a given municipality in that case Bratunac precluded a certain disposition and I'll read you the question and answer. "And how do you think that 30 per cent Serbs can force 70 per cent Muslims in Bratunac to do this job?" Your answer: "We're talking Bratunac, right, not Vlasenica? I think somebody mentioned Vlasenica earlier. They had the backing of the JNA. They had paramilitaries available to them. It was, as I say, at the point of a gun and I think subsequent events in Bratunac" -- I'm -- pardon me, "in the period after this supposed agreement bear this out. And it's not my role to go into what those were, but I think it also makes all the more empty and all the more just -- it makes it into a mere gesture the statement about the rights of other peoples in the course of the Serb seizure of power." So your answer to that question whether a demographic imbalance precluded a disposition desired by the Serbs was known. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard could I turn to 65 ter number 00091, an extract or excerpt from the Bosnian Serb Assembly Session of 28 August 1995, a speech by Dr. Karadzic. And the page in the English version is 68 and in the Serbian version page 87. Are you familiar with the 53rd Bosnian Serb Assembly Session and the context of this session?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, please. In the English, if we could go to about three lines up from the bottom of page 68. Thank you. And in the B/C/S about -- it's about 17 lines up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I would like to take you to the passage that begins: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us ..." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It begins with the word "we" on the third line up from the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So again: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves." If we could move over, please, in the English, "and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours ..." Have you seen all -- have you been able to read the passage that I've been reading to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is this consistent, this passage excerpted from a speech by Dr. Karadzic, with your articulated view as regards whether a demographic imbalance precluded a disposition desired by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the phenomenon to which I was referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P980.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, that intercept that Your Honour, Judge Morrison, asked me about, some quick checking by my colleagues, they've informed me the date of that intercept is 27 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you remember the questionnaire handed over by the accused, whether you would agree to certain facts relating to the events that happened in Slovenia and Croatia, I wonder whether you had some time to go over the questions and whether you would be agreeable to those facts or there are some -- any observations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have lost track of that document somewhere here. I think I left it two days or three days ago. I did review the document the evening that you gave it to me, and found that there were about five or six assertions that I could concur with, either in whole or in part. But the vast majority of -- and I could tell you what they are really enough, but the vast majority of the statements that are presented in this document I neither have the knowledge of or with me the resources to concur with or to dissent from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your -- is your response related to the content of the decision of some courts or ... ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the -- virtually the -- most of the assertions pertain to rulings by the constitutional court, interpretations by one court or another, and specific acts that were promulgated by either a republic Assembly or the Federal Assembly. And I'm simply not in a position to verify or deny those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even as to the fact that whether such and such ruling took place at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the case in each ruling. There is a couple of provisions, as I say, that I can affirm very briefly number 2, the first sentence -- I don't have -- I agree with that. Then have the -- had the information to be able to verify that. Certainly number 3 I concur with. Number 4. Number 6, the first sentence. Number 9, the first sentence. Understanding that the term "illegally" is not mine, but the term actually used in the Presidency's proclamation. And I believe there's one or two more here that -- as I go through that pertain to Croatia. It was entertaining bedtime reading, Your Honour. Number 44, concur. The first sentence of number 58. The first sentence of number 59 and first sentence of number 70. I believe that concludes the points that I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm amazed by your memory, Doctor. Thank you. That concludes your testimony here. Thank you again for coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your courtesies to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the indulgence of the interpreters, we go to ten past. I understand that there's some issues for you to raise, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll be very brief, they pertain to the next witness, Richard Philipps. We have asked OLAD to authorise payment for our expert witness so he can be present in courtroom as the Trial Chamber authorised on the 2nd of June. OLAD has denied any funding for that. Since Dr. Karadzic is indigent, that means that unless that decision is reversed he wouldn't be able to take advantage of the permission given by the Chamber. We have appealed that to the Registrar today and we would intend to raise that with the Trial Chamber as well if that matter is denied by the Registrar. All of this may have an impact with Mr. Philipps commencing his testimony on Tuesday, if, in fact, we're not able to resolve the matter before then and I wished to bring that to your attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have anything to say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We do consider that it has or should have any impact on the witness's upcoming testimony. This matter has been before the Defence for a considerable period of time. The witness has been scheduled for a very long time. All this material has been available for a very long time, and I would also note that this is a 92 ter witness, so the Defence has been aware of the nature of the -- the bulk of the examination-in-chief also for an extremely long time. Finally, there's no basis for, in our submission, Your Honour, any suggestion of a postponement. I think there is, perhaps, a risk of conflating the opportunity presented by the Court's ruling with some form of requirement or right that is at issue. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do not take any position in relation to the issue of reimbursement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that matter we leave -- I mean, let this matter play itself out in due course. But in due course, it's properly right it should have no impact on the scheduling and hearing of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. When we issued the decision or -- granting the request from the Defence to permit the presence of Mr. Radinovic, if my pronunciation is correct, the Chamber was of the view that his presence would be of assistance to both the Defence and the Chamber. So it was reasonable to assume at the time that the Chamber's decision to permit his presence can have no effect if financial assistance would not be available. So I would recommend Registrar to make decision as soon as possible, so as to limit the impact of this issue on the proceedings. And the Chamber will also see what it can do outside the courtroom so that the positive resolution can be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think from the letter of OLAD that those kind of comments will resolve the issue. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. -- Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's really directed to Dr. Karadzic because I'm slightly concerned that you might, not being a trained lawyer, have misdirected yourself to some degree to the effect of expert evidence and the requirement to challenge each and every part of an expert's report. An expert's report is a report based upon that expert's opinion. Of course you can challenge that opinion where you disagree with it, but the fact that you haven't challenged an opinion doesn't turn that opinion into undisputed fact. And the opportunity is always there for you, during the Defence case or perhaps even in respect of the testimony of other witnesses, to deal with issues that you feel you haven't dealt with with Dr. Donia. I think it's important for you to realise that the mere fact that you may not have raised an issue with Dr. Donia does not, in itself, mean that that issue has somehow become set in stone and is not capable of another interpretation when viewed in the light of other evidence that you may choose to bring in due course. My remarks are not intended to encourage you to bring other evidence, but to resolve any worries that you may have as a result of misunderstanding or potentially misunderstanding the nature and effect of opinion evidence, which is what expert evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Morrison. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to rise but thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I can -- I could raise the matter later. I would simply note Dr. Karadzic raised the question of context of the excerpts report, and I would remind the Court that it was the Prosecution that raised the issue of the agreement it reached with the Defence to suggest the joint submission or agreement to the submission of the Assembly sessions referenced in Dr. Donia's report. If the Court wishes, we can provide a list of those sessions if it wishes to consider that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's quite recommendable, speaking for myself. Thank you again and I hope everybody will have a very restful, peaceful, and refreshing weekend. Tuesday afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.11 p.m.,
